longQuestions: A discrete uniform distribution gives equal probability to each of k possible values x₁, …, x_k: f(x) = 1/k.
Example: the number on a fair die, f(x) = 1/6 for x = 1, …, 6. Mean = (k+1)/2 and variance = (k²−1)/12 for values 1 to k.
Random digits are the digits 0–9 each occurring with equal probability 1/10, independently of one another.

Random numbers are numbers formed from random digits; a random number generator is a device or computer program (e.g. RAND in a calculator/computer) that produces such numbers; a random number table is a printed table of random digits arranged in rows and columns, used to select random samples.
Number the colleges from 001 to 206 (three-digit numbers).
Start at any point of the random number table and read three-digit numbers in a fixed direction (row or column).
Select a college whenever the number lies between 001 and 206; ignore numbers above 206 and repetitions; continue until 10 different colleges are selected — these form the random sample.
i) Bernoulli experiment — a trial with only two possible outcomes, success or failure, with P(success) = p.
ii) Bernoulli random variable — X = 1 for success and 0 for failure.
iii) Binomial experiment — n independent Bernoulli trials with the same probability of success p.
iv) Binomial random variable — X = number of successes in n trials, X = 0, 1, …, n.
Bernoulli distribution: f(x) = pˣq¹⁻ˣ, x = 0, 1, where q = 1 − p.
Mean E(X) = 0·q + 1·p = p; E(X²) = p, so variance = p − p² = pq; standard deviation = √(pq).

i) A binomial experiment consists of n repeated trials with conditions: (1) fixed number of trials n; (2) each trial has two outcomes, success and failure; (3) probability of success p is constant; (4) trials are independent.
ii) For X ~ b(n, p), f(x) = ⁿCₓ pˣ qⁿ⁻ˣ. Mean = Σ x f(x) = np (taking np out and summing the remaining binomial terms to 1); E[X(X−1)] = n(n−1)p², so variance = n(n−1)p² + np − n²p² = npq.
P(X = x) = ⁵Cₓ (3/8)ˣ (5/8)⁵⁻ˣ, with denominator 8⁵ = 32768.

a) A binomial distribution gives the probability of x successes in n independent trials each with success probability p: f(x) = ⁿCₓ pˣ qⁿ⁻ˣ, x = 0, 1, …, n. It arises in practice whenever a fixed number of independent two-outcome trials is made — e.g. number of defective items in a sample, number of heads in coin tosses, number of patients cured.
b) Mean = np and S.D = √(npq) (derived by E(X) = np and E[X(X−1)] = n(n−1)p², giving variance npq).
Hypergeometric experiment — n items are drawn without replacement from a finite population of N items of which k are 'successes' and N − k 'failures'; the trials are dependent.
Hypergeometric random variable — X = number of successes among the n items drawn.
Hypergeometric probability distribution — P(X = x) = ᵏCₓ·ᴺ⁻ᵏCₙ₋ₓ / ᴺCₙ, x = max(0, n−N+k), …, min(n, k); mean nk/N and variance n(k/N)(1 − k/N)(N − n)/(N − 1).
For a hypergeometric distribution (n items drawn without replacement from N items of which k are successes): f(x) = ᵏCₓ·ᴺ⁻ᵏCₙ₋ₓ / ᴺCₙ.
Mean = n·k/N.
Variance = n·(k/N)·(1 − k/N)·(N − n)/(N − 1).
N = 11 balls, k = 7 black, n = 5 drawn; P(X = x) = ⁷Cₓ·⁴C₅₋ₓ / ¹¹C₅ with ¹¹C₅ = 462; X can be 1 to 5 (there are only 4 white balls).
